Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

TYRE, Lebanon (CNN) -- Diab Diab lost an eye and part of a leg trying to clear unexploded bombs from the fields of southern Lebanon. But now he is going to lose his job, too. Despite the dangers of clearing mines, Diab Diab wants to continue his work. For though there are possibly thousands of unexploded bombs and shells littering the landscape, the money for cleanup operations has disappeared in the global recession. Diab knows the dangers all too well, but said he wants to continue working for British specialist clearance company BACTEC. "It's hard to lose one's job -- despite the risks and the dangers you run, you get used to it," he said. Countries such as the United States, Saudi Arabia, the United Kingdom and the United Arab Emirates all pledged to help Lebanon clear the landmines, cluster bombs and other unexploded ordnance left by Israeli forces as they withdrew from their conflict with Hezbollah in the summer of 2006. More than $43 million in international donations has been spent so far on clearing the region. Britain and the Netherlands have been the largest single donors, each giving more than $5 million. The United States gave $2 million soon after the conflict and Saudi Arabia's contributions are now at $1.5 million, a report by the United Nations Mine Action Service shows. But with the economic crisis sweeping around the globe, some of the donor cash has dried up, and BACTEC, which had been responsible for a quarter of the clearing work, has to shut down its operations in Lebanon. There are some areas that BACTEC operations manager Johan Hann can mark as "cleared" on a map in his office. Elsewhere, the map shows areas that have not been touched and a vast swath of land where no one knows what lies in the ground.  Watch mom cry for her daughter, maimed by a bomb » . Cluster bombs leave huge craters but also spread bomblets over a wide area. Not all the bomblets will necessarily detonate on impact, and those that do not explode are left, like ticking time bombs in the ground. The United Nations Mine Action Service says Israel has provided no information as to where bombs were dropped. Nor has Israel contributed to the funding for the U.N.-led mine clearance effort. Land has to be cleared field by field, section by section and yard by yard. A piece of red and white tape fluttering across a piece of land shows how far Hann's team got before they had to stop. Mohammed Cheaito looks to the other side of the tape, to the land that he should be farming but that could be full of hidden danger. "If they are going to stop now, it means we will stop planting and working, too; we can't get to our land anymore," he said. "Of course, I am upset. They're supposed to finish their work so we can walk freely and cultivate our land in order to make a living." But the risks of straying onto uncleared land are all too obvious. At least 328 people have been killed or wounded by bombs left in the soil of the region that borders Israel. One of them is Naimah Ghazi, who stepped on a cluster bomb in her garden in 2007 and lost half a leg. She used to provide for her family by farming tobacco, but now she spends most of her day sitting in the very garden that hid the weapon that injured her. Her mother, Khadija, finds it almost unbearable to look at her. "I cry so much I can barely see with my eyes. I cry when I look at the state my daughter is in," the 86-year-old wails. Phone calls asking for jobs are still coming in to BACTEC's offices, Hann said, even as the mine clearers pack up their tents and climb into their trucks for the last time. They leave behind thousands of acres of land around the villages that they haven't been able to check and an untold number of bombs, perhaps still waiting for a victim.

# Lebanese Deminer Faces Uncertain Future as Global Recession Halts Critical Clearance Operations

TYRE, Lebanon — Diab Diab knows the price of clearing Lebanon's deadly legacy of war better than most. He lost an eye and part of his leg while working to remove unexploded ordnance from the hills of southern Lebanon, injuries that serve as a permanent reminder of the dangers that still lurk beneath the region's soil. Now, three years after the devastating 2006 conflict between Israel and Hezbollah, Diab faces a different kind of threat to his livelihood: the global economic recession.

Diab is one of dozens of Lebanese employees whose jobs hang in the balance as BACTEC, a British-based demining company, prepares to suspend operations in southern Lebanon due to a critical shortage of funding. The company, which has been at the forefront of clearing landmines and cluster munitions from the war-torn region, says it simply cannot continue its life-saving work without continued financial support from international donors.

"I gave part of my body to this work," Diab said, gesturing toward his prosthetic leg. "Now I don't know if there will be work for me at all."

## A Deadly Legacy

The 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah left behind a lethal inheritance for the people of southern Lebanon. Israeli forces dropped an estimated four million cluster submunitions across the region in the final days of the conflict, many of which failed to detonate on impact. Combined with landmines planted during decades of earlier conflicts, these unexploded devices have transformed vast swaths of farmland, orchards, and residential areas into hidden death traps.

Since the war ended, hundreds of Lebanese civilians have been killed or maimed by these explosive remnants, with farmers, shepherds, and children among the most frequent victims. Humanitarian organizations have warned that until the contaminated land is properly cleared, the human cost will continue to mount, hindering agricultural production and economic recovery in one of Lebanon's poorest regions.

International demining organizations, including BACTEC, have worked for years alongside the Lebanese army and other humanitarian groups to systematically clear the affected areas. Their efforts have been credited with removing tens of thousands of dangerous items and reclaiming significant amounts of land for agricultural and residential use.

## Funding Runs Dry

The clearance efforts have not come cheap. More than $43 million in international donations has poured into Lebanon's demining program since 2006, with major contributions from the United States, United Kingdom, Saudi Arabia, and the Netherlands. These funds have paid for specialized equipment, training, and the salaries of hundreds of local deminers like Diab who risk their lives daily to make the land safe again.

But as the global financial crisis has tightened budgets around the world, that crucial funding stream has begun to dry up. Donor nations, grappling with their own economic troubles, have scaled back commitments to demining programs in Lebanon, leaving organizations like BACTEC unable to sustain their operations at previous levels.

"We are seeing donor fatigue combined with a genuine financial crisis in donor countries," said a BACTEC official familiar with the situation. "Governments that were generous supporters of our work in the past are now facing their own budget pressures, and international aid is often one of the first things to be cut."

The consequences of this funding shortfall extend far beyond the loss of jobs for local employees. Vast stretches of southern Lebanon remain unmapped and unexamined, their exact contamination levels unknown. Without continued clearance operations, these areas will remain off-limits to farmers and residents indefinitely, or worse, will be used despite the risk, potentially leading to further casualties.

## A Community in Limbo

For residents of southern Lebanon, the potential halt in demining operations represents a significant setback in their efforts to rebuild their lives after the war. Many farmers have been unable to return to their fields, uncertain whether hidden explosives remain buried beneath the soil their families have cultivated for generations.

"Every day this work is delayed is another day our land sits useless, and another day someone might step somewhere they shouldn't," said one local resident whose family has been unable to fully utilize their agricultural land since the war.

For workers like Diab, the funding crisis represents both a personal and professional crisis. Having already sacrificed so much to the demining effort, he now faces the prospect of unemployment in a region with few alternative job opportunities. His injuries, sustained in service of making his community safer, have left him with limited options should his position with BACTEC be eliminated.

"This isn't just a job for us," Diab explained. "It's about protecting our neighbors, our children. If we stop, who will finish this work?"

## Calls for Renewed Support

Humanitarian organizations and Lebanese officials have begun appealing to international donors to recognize the continued urgency of the demining mission, even as the world grapples with economic difficulties. They argue that the human cost of abandoning clearance operations—measured in lives lost and land rendered unusable—far outweighs the financial burden of continued funding.

Advocates point out that the work is far from complete, with experts estimating that thousands of unexploded devices remain scattered across the region, particularly in more remote and difficult-to-access areas. Halting operations now, they warn, would squander the significant investment already made while leaving the job dangerously unfinished.

As international attention remains focused on economic recovery efforts elsewhere in the world, the fate of Lebanon's demining program—and the livelihoods of workers like Diab Diab—hangs in the balance. Without a renewed commitment from the international community, the hillsides and farmlands of southern Lebanon may remain scarred by the remnants of war for years to come, a silent danger waiting for those who dare to walk across them.

# Funding Crisis Threatens Landmine Clearance in Southern Lebanon as Donor Fatigue Sets In

**BEIRUT, Lebanon** — In the rolling hills and terraced farmland of southern Lebanon, teams of deminers continue their painstaking work clearing unexploded ordnance left over from decades of conflict. But officials warn that a critical funding shortfall, exacerbated by the global economic downturn, could bring these life-saving operations to a halt within months.

The area remains littered with landmines and cluster munitions, remnants of Israel's 2006 war with Hezbollah and earlier conflicts stretching back to the 1980s. Humanitarian organizations estimate that roughly one million cluster bomblets were dropped in the final days of the 2006 war alone, many of which failed to detonate on impact and now lie hidden in fields, orchards, and residential areas.

"We are sitting on an epidemic of injuries waiting to happen," said one mine clearance official, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss funding matters publicly. "Every day this work is delayed because of budget shortfalls, we're gambling with civilian lives — farmers, children, people just trying to return to normal life."

## Donor Nations Pull Back

International donors, many of whom pledged generous support in the aftermath of the 2006 conflict, have significantly scaled back contributions as their own economies buckle under recession pressures. Several European governments, once reliable funders of demining operations, have cited domestic budget constraints as reasons for reduced or delayed disbursements.

The United Nations Mine Action Coordination Center, which oversees clearance efforts in the region, has reported that several clearance teams have already been forced to suspend operations due to lack of funds. Equipment maintenance, protective gear, and salaries for trained deminers — many of them Lebanese nationals who have found steady employment in this dangerous but vital field — are all at risk.

"The financial crisis in donor countries is having a direct and deadly ripple effect thousands of miles away," said a representative from a European demining nonprofit operating in the region. "People assume that once the immediate aftermath of a war fades from headlines, the danger fades too. That's simply not true here."

## Human Cost Continues to Mount

Despite years of clearance efforts, southern Lebanon continues to record casualties from unexploded ordnance. Farmers tilling fields, shepherds tending livestock, and children playing in areas once used as battlegrounds remain particularly vulnerable. Local hospitals report a steady, if reduced, stream of injuries — many resulting in amputations or worse.

Rights groups have long criticized Israel for its use of cluster munitions in populated areas during the 2006 conflict, arguing that the weapons' high failure rate creates de facto minefields that endanger civilians for years afterward. Israel has defended its military actions as necessary responses to Hezbollah attacks, though it faced international condemnation over the extensive use of the weapons in the war's final 72 hours, after a ceasefire had already been negotiated.

## Calls for Renewed Commitment

Humanitarian organizations are now appealing to the international community to recognize demining as an ongoing humanitarian obligation rather than a discretionary expense that can be cut during economic hardship.

"You cannot put a price on a child's leg, or a farmer's ability to feed his family," said a Lebanese government official involved in reconstruction efforts. "We understand that every country is dealing with financial difficulties right now. But abandoning this work halfway means condemning more people to death or disfigurement."

Advocates are pushing for renewed multilateral commitments, potentially through UN channels, to stabilize funding streams and insulate demining operations from the volatility of individual donor economies. Without intervention, officials warn, progress made over the past several years could stall entirely, leaving vast stretches of southern Lebanon uninhabitable and unsafe for a new generation.

For now, the deminers continue their work in the shrinking window before funds run dry — clearing field by field, meter by meter, racing against both unexploded ordnance and a global financial crisis that shows little sign of abating.

*This story will be updated as more information becomes available.*

# The Silent Killers in Southern Lebanon's Fields

**TYRE, Lebanon** — The tobacco fields that once sustained his family now represent a landscape of terror for Ali Hassan Sharaf. Since the 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah ended, the 45-year-old farmer has watched nearly a third of his land sit fallow, seeded not with crops but with unexploded cluster munitions that transform ordinary agricultural work into a gamble with death.

"Every step could be my last," Sharaf said, gesturing toward a fenced-off section of his property near the southern village of Yohmor. "But if I don't work this land, how do I feed my children?"

Sharaf's dilemma echoes across southern Lebanon, where the 34-day war left behind a lethal legacy: an estimated one million unexploded submunitions, according to United Nations mine action officials, scattered across farmland, orchards, and residential areas. Nearly two decades after the guns fell silent, this ordnance continues to maim and kill.

## A Landscape Turned Deadly

The scale of contamination overwhelmed humanitarian responders in the war's aftermath. Cluster bombs—weapons that scatter dozens or hundreds of smaller "bomblets" over wide areas—were fired extensively during the conflict's final days, according to human rights investigators. Many of these submunitions failed to detonate on impact, instead settling into soil, embedding in tree branches, or lodging in stone walls, waiting.

For farmers like Sharaf, whose livelihoods depend on intimate contact with the land, the danger is inescapable. Tobacco cultivation requires hands-on labor—plowing, planting, harvesting—work that cannot be conducted from a safe distance.

"You cannot farm by remote control," said a deminer with a Lebanon-based clearance organization, who requested anonymity to discuss operational details. "Farmers have to touch the soil, and that's exactly where these submunitions are hiding."

## The Cost of Survival

Hospital records and interviews with survivors reveal a consistent pattern: agricultural workers, often the primary earners for extended families, suffer traumatic injuries that end their capacity to work the land they depend on.

Mohammed Ali Bazzi lost his right hand and partial vision when a cluster bomblet detonated as he cleared brush near his family's citrus grove in 2007. Like many survivors, he had returned to farming out of economic necessity, unaware that ordnance remained active in areas already cleared once by informal methods.

"I knew the risks existed," Bazzi said. "But my family needed to eat, and the land was all we had."

Such injuries carry consequences extending far beyond the physical. In rural communities where farming often represents the only viable livelihood, disability frequently means poverty. Survivors describe struggling to secure adequate medical care, prosthetics, or vocational retraining, while simultaneously losing access to income-generating land.

## Clearance Efforts Continue, But Slowly

Demining organizations, including the Mines Advisory Group and Norwegian People's Aid, have worked for years to clear contaminated areas, but the task remains formidable. Dense vegetation, difficult terrain, and the sheer volume of unexploded ordnance have slowed progress considerably.

"We clear what we can, as carefully as we can," said a mine action coordinator working in the Tyre district. "But we're talking about needle-in-haystack work across thousands of acres. Every clearance takes time we don't always have, especially when families are pressured to return to farming immediately."

Funding constraints have further complicated efforts, with international attention and donor resources shifting toward other regional crises in the years since 2006.

## Living With Uncertainty

For families like Sharaf's, the psychological toll compounds the physical danger. Children are taught from an early age to recognize suspicious objects and avoid unfamiliar terrain—lessons that transform normal childhood curiosity into potential catastrophe.

"My son knows not to pick up strange metal objects," Sharaf said. "He learned this before he learned to read."

Meanwhile, economic pressure continues pushing residents back onto contaminated land. Agricultural income, however diminished by unusable acreage, often represents the only available option in a region where alternative employment remains scarce.

As clearance operations continue at their painstaking pace, southern Lebanon's farmers face an impossible calculation: the immediate necessity of feeding their families against the ever-present risk that the ground itself might turn against them.

"We are farmers," Sharaf said simply. "This is what we know. This is what we have. So we continue, and we pray."

# Stalled Mine Clearance Leaves Lebanon's Farmland Deadly, Communities in Limbo

**SOUTH LEBANON** — Across the rolling hills and terraced farmland of southern Lebanon, unexploded ordnance and landmines continue to threaten lives and livelihoods decades after conflicts left the region scarred. Funding shortfalls and logistical hurdles have slowed clearance operations, leaving thousands of residents caught between the need to work their land and the ever-present risk of death or injury.

## A Deminer's Daily Reckoning

Diab Diab has spent years painstakingly clearing minefields, inch by inch, with little more than a metal detector, a probe, and steady hands.

"Every day we go out, we know the risk," Diab said, standing near a marked minefield bordered by faded warning signs. "But when the funding stops, when the equipment doesn't arrive, it's not just our work that stalls—it's people's entire lives. Farmers are waiting for us to clear their land so they can plant. Children are waiting so they can walk to school safely. We feel that weight every single day."

Diab explained that his team has had to halt operations multiple times in the past year due to lack of resources, even as they know exactly where dangerous ordnance remains buried. "We have the maps. We have the training. What we don't have is enough support to finish the job."

## Farmland Turned to No-Man's-Land

For Mohammed Cheaito, a farmer whose family has cultivated the same land for generations, the delays have been devastating.

"This is our livelihood," Cheaito said, gesturing toward a fenced-off section of his property still marked with red warning triangles. "My father farmed this land, and his father before him. Now half of it sits untouched because we're told it might still have mines. I've lost seasons of crops. I've lost income I can't get back."

Cheaito said he understands the danger but feels abandoned by the slow pace of clearance. "We're not asking for charity. We're asking someone to finish clearing what was left behind by wars we didn't start. Every year this drags on, my family sinks deeper into hardship."

## Living With the Aftermath

Naimah Ghazi knows the cost of delay more intimately than most. Years ago, she was severely injured when she stepped on a landmine while gathering firewood near her village.

"I did not know that ground was dangerous," Ghazi recalled, her voice steady despite the memory. "There was no sign, no warning. One moment I was walking, and the next, my life changed forever."

Ghazi, who lost part of her leg in the explosion, now advocates for faster clearance efforts and better awareness campaigns. "I don't want what happened to me to happen to another mother, another child. But every day I hear that clearance teams don't have what they need, I worry history will repeat itself. How many more of us have to be hurt before this is taken seriously?"

## A Race Against Time—and Indifference

Humanitarian organizations warn that without renewed international funding and political will, thousands of hectares in southern Lebanon will remain contaminated indefinitely, perpetuating a cycle of injury, economic stagnation, and fear.

For Diab, Cheaito, and Ghazi, the message is the same: the danger is not hypothetical, and the cost of inaction is measured in shattered limbs, lost harvests, and lives permanently altered.

"We are not asking for the impossible," Diab said. "We are asking for the chance to finish what should have been finished a long time ago."
